title: US set for largest mass visa revocation in history targeting up to 200,000 foreigners, officials say
description: The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States.  If it happ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States. If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history and would likely face legal challenges.

Unless challenged or revised, the State Department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by The Associated Press and two U.S. officials. The action will be taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," said State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott.

He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying "as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."

The revocations would not necessarily result in their immediate deportation, the officials said. Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorized but would lose their status as business or tourism travelers, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the revocations are not final yet.

Since President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants — demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds for the processing of visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.

In a social media post on Monday, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the United States and then apply for asylum.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Landau wrote on X. "Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law." Landau cited the case of a Colombian citizen who came to the U.S. in 2015 on a tourist visa and then applied for asylum.

B1 visas are generally issued for business trips and B2 visas are generally issued for tourism, family visits or medical care. It was not immediately clear from the documents or the officials how many of these visa holders are seeking or have sought asylum in the United States and would be affected by the revocations.

Current applicants for B1 and B2 visas are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum in the United States and prove that they intend to return to their home countries.

In the past 18 months, the State Department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunken driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against U.S. policies, particularly in the Middle East.

The administration has also moved to crack down on so-called birth tourism, a practice the administration claims is used by foreign pregnant women to come to the United States to give birth so that their child will benefit from birthright citizenship. Trump has tried several times to end birthright citizenship, but those challenges have been rejected by courts, including the Supreme Court.

The State Department documents obtained by the AP suggest screening of current B1 and B2 visa holders began after the State Department received information about asylum requests from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

title: Canadians are doubling down on their American boycott after Trump's latest tariffs
description: Canadians recommitted to their boycott of American goods and travel. "Some people got a little lazy with it," one Canadian said.
fullText:
Canadians recommitted to their boycott of American goods and travel as a trade war with the US escalates.

On Saturday, the US tariffs on some Canadian goods took effect, and Trump threatened additional auto tariffs.

Canadians spoke out across social media. Some told Business Insider they were committed to not buying American products.

Canadians have long been boycotting American goods. Then came the latest wave of tariffs.

Trade talks between the US and Canada fell apart on Friday, and the US enforced a 50% tariff on some Canadian goods the following day. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney quickly proposed dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs.

Many Canadians were already fed up with their neighbors down south. Some previously chose to stop buying American products; others suspended their travel to America.

On social media and in interviews with Business Insider, Canadians say that the breakdown in talks has reinvigorated their push to stop buying US goods.

Carney quickly worked to turn the tariffs into a unifying force.

"Canada has what the world wants," he wrote on Friday night. "We will not allow any nation to determine our future. We will set our own course to keep Canada strong for all."

It's hard to know whether the messaging works, though there are some signs. Eurasia Group founder Ian Bremmer wrote on X that he had never seen Canadians from all political viewpoints "so angry" with the US.

Time to launch a full blown no holds barred boycott of American products and services. Trump wants a fight, let's bring it. 

Who's with me?

— Bruce Anderson (@bruceanderson) August 23, 2026

Tyler Black keeps hearing about it. The 49-year-old child psychiatrist told Business Insider that, if you went for a walk in his hometown of Vancouver, there was a 50/50 chance you'd hear about the tariffs.

"I'm not kidding," he said. "Random conversations I'm walking by are talking about Trump and Carney, and what America just did. We're feeling very attacked."

Black is one of many Canadians who say they have boycotted American goods since President Donald Trump's reelection. Over the weekend, more people were pledging to join the boycott, he said. "It's what we're all talking about."

On X, users are reviving the #BoycottUSA tag. Redditors posted infographics about supporting "Buy Canadian" during the tariffs, and Europeans wondered if they should join in. TikToks cheering on retaliatory tariffs got thousands of likes.

Economic boycotts rarely have a material effect on the business or businesses in the crosshairs. Still, there are some cases, like the Target boycott movement. And a boycott can ruffle feathers. In July, the White House called Canada's treatment of US products "discriminatory."

🇨🇦Canada is asking the rest of the world to join us in boycotting all American products. Thank You ❤️

— Lucy 🇨🇦 (@TheBlueGem3) August 23, 2026

Trump has been in office for over a year, and he's spoken frequently about annexing Canada. That's a long time to swear off US goods.

There are some signs of the anti-US sentiment going strong, like soccer fans booing the American national anthem. There are other signs of a bottoming out, like travel data between Canada and the US.

Tyler said he hoped the tariffs would reverse that travel trend.

"I have no doubt that it's going to fall back down again," he said. "I think Canadians are going to take this very patriotically."

Despite our political differences:

Don't buy American. Buy Canadian
Don't buy from stores who make that difficult. 
Be united in resistance to Trump
Call out the treacherous

This is our moment to show the world who we are

— Cheri DiNovo (@CheriDiNovo) August 22, 2026

Tina Garrett, a 45-year-old writer from Toronto, has also been boycotting since long before the tariffs went into effect. Still, she saw signs that the recent news would reinvigorate the movement.

"Some people got a little lazy with it," she said. "I think it will renew the boycott for a lot of people."

title: Business-class fliers love sliding doors — but they’re causing a nuisance for airlines and planemakers
description: Airlines are competing for the fanciest business class following the boom in premium travel, but new suites require rigorous certification testing.
fullText:
The rise in premium travel is causing frustrations for airlines and manufacturers.

Fancy new business-class seats need to go through rigorous certification testing.

Airplanes have been stuck at factories or flown with empty business class cabins.

More travelers are shelling out for the best airplane seats amid a boom in premium travel, driving airlines to develop increasingly complex business-class seats — some of which are proving to be a headache for carriers and manufacturers alike.

Since COVID-19, airlines have been packing their planes with fancy new cabins as they try to attract more deep-pocketed customers. In April, United Airlines rolled out an airplane with 64 business-class seats. Delta Air Lines plans to debut its Airbus A350-1000 next year with 53 business-class suites.

But new seat designs must undergo rigorous certification by aviation regulators. And ongoing approval delays are derailing plans, leaving airplanes stuck at factories awaiting delivery and, in some cases, flying with their highly profitable business-class doors locked open or the seats off-limits to passengers altogether.

Sliding doors are a frequent hurdle for certification. First introduced by Emirates in 2003 to give first-class passengers extra privacy, they are now essentially de rigueur in business class.

However, regulators must be certain that these doors won't impede passengers during an evacuation.

When American Airlines started flying the Airbus A321XLR last December, it had to keep the sliding doors locked open until the Federal Aviation Administration certified them seven months later. The same issue befell United Airlines when it debuted its new Polaris suites on the Boeing 787-9 in April. These were made by the Boeing subsidiary Elevate Aircraft Seating, based on a customizable design similar to one used by several airlines.

"They all have exactly this same door design, and we're still struggling every time to get them certified, including the ones that are flying already," Sascha Manitz, a sales director at Elevate, told Business Insider during the UK's Farnborough Airshow in July. "It seems like the goalposts are moving all the time."

In a statement, the FAA said it is "engaged with seat and aircraft manufacturers to maintain clear communication throughout the certification lifecycle," and collaborating with international partners and authorities to "streamline the approval process."

United's Polaris suites were eventually certified, and the first sliding doors unlocked in early August. Air India has also locked its new 787 business-class doors open, but it's still navigating FAA certification.

fullText:
Buc-ee's opened its first Arkansas location in Benton on Aug. 17, continuing the beaver-branded travel center's expansion out of its Texas stomping grounds.

The location is expected to bring more than 200 jobs to the city and will occupy 74,000 square feet with 120 fueling stations, according to a Buc-ee's news release. It added that the starting wage for employees is "well above minimum wage" but did not specify what it is.

Buc-ee's opened its first locations in Ohio and Arizona this year. In 2025, it opened its first location in Virginia and a year earlier, it debuted in Colorado. The company anticipates adding inaugural locations in Louisiana, Kansas and Wisconsin by the end of 2027.

The travel center, founded in 1982, has become one of the Lone Star State's most recognized exports. The sprawling gas stations have a cult-like following centered on their preternaturally clean restrooms and unique culinary offerings.

The Benton location is 58th Buc-ee's location in the country.

Here's where Buc-ee's is slated to open next.

Crissy Gonzales, Buc-ee's media coordinator, previously said in an email to USA TODAY that the Murfreesboro, Tennessee location will open on Nov. 16.

The company's contact page lists the following locations as opening without specific grand opening dates:

Hardeeville, South Carolina: 2031

USA TODAY has reached out to Buc-ee's for opening dates for these locations.

Buc-ee's has drawn controversy in recent weeks for a string of lawsuits tied to its trademarks.

Most recently, the company sued Beaver's Mini Mart, a small corner store located in the middle of a neighborhood in Beavercreek, Ohio, a suburb of Dayton.

The Cincinnati Enquirer, part of the USA TODAY Network, reported that despite the mini mart having no gas pumps and being miles from the nearest interstate, Buc-ee's says its customers may be confused by the mini mart's logo, which features a smiling beaver standing tall next to the store's name in a red-letter font.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has said Buc-ee's should drop its "ridiculous" lawsuit against Beaver's Mini Mart.

fullText:
The Guardian’s deputy editor of social platforms on the demand from high-profile people and brands for help in harnessing the power of TikTok

I didn’t want to work in social media. If you’d asked 15-year-old me my dream job, I might have said foreign correspondent, or maybe travel writer. So you can imagine my surprise to now find myself giving these very colleagues advice on how to get the best selfie angle or write the sharpest TikTok ‘hook’.

But taking a job as the Guardian’s deputy editor of social platforms, may prove to be one of my smartest career moves if the current job market is to be believed.

You don’t need to be a digital native to have noticed the way that celebrities, brands and, yes, the prime minister, are taking their social media game seriously these days.

Westminster watchers keeping an eye on the government jobs board to get an idea of the type of people Burnham’s operation wants to recruit, noticed no less than five newly created roles for social media professionals – the most senior of them earning a touch under £70,000 per year.

Burnham’s wholesale commitment to feeding the algorithm may feel like a relative novelty on this side of the pond, but social media has been a political battleground in the US for much longer.

Early in Trump’s presidency, outgoing press secretary Karoline Leavitt could regularly be seen recapping the administration’s “successes” with the catchy “Maga minute”, and New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s masterful use of social comms is the envy of politicians the world over.

But while it’s true that the internet game requires a charismatic personality, backstage there is a squad of editors, producers and strategists making the whole thing sing. That’s where we come in.

My journey into social media began when my team at CNN took over producing for the TikTok channel in 2023. I realised that’s where audiences, including myself, really were.

If you hear the word TikTok and think it’s just dance trends and memes, think again. My job involved getting phone calls from war zones asking if I had what I needed and being sent selfies from craters. When I left earlier this year we had grown the account to almost 12 million followers.

Now mainstream media is trying to beat content creators at their own game. Oxford’s Reuters Institute this year reported that social and video networks have overtaken news websites and apps by audience share. The BBC has even hired a gen z whisperer.

As with most things in the world of social media, this change has happened rapidly, one of the consequences of that change is that there is really no such thing as a “traditional route” into the industry.

Lauren Spearman is an accidental influencer who found a TikTok following, now at 62,000, while documenting her own frustrations finding a full-time role in marketing. She now enjoys a successful freelance career consulting with the benefit of two decades of experience in social. She says she’s seen a recent shift in businesses hiring for content creators.

“Social is often infantilised but it is business critical,” Spearman said. And she’s right, the trope for years has been that interns are running the accounts of your favourite businesses, but you’re much more likely to find a savvy millennial with a marketing degree behind a brand’s X feed.

What remains to be seen is if C-suites and business leaders really understand the needs of their audiences, or those they’re hiring to cater to them. “The biggest challenge has always been educating up,” said Spearman, noting that she often sees junior roles with small salaries but large scopes and unclear remits.

“A lot of times I’ll go into businesses and there is no strategy that ladders back into what the business is doing,” she said. Let’s not forget that your social producers are often on the frontline of customer interactions and what most consumers see but often still misunderstood and sidelined.

Social media can, of course, be a place for slop; for fearmongering, for misinformation. But the vast majority of good actors are on it as a place to be entertained, informed and even exercise their civic duties.

In many ways it’s still the closest to a global town square we’ve got, fraught with algorithmic problems and regulatory loopholes as it might be. It’s time to start taking the people behind these accounts seriously.

title: Mamdani's team said NYPD would accompany his wife on Middle East vacation — cops say that's not true
description: The NYPD denied it would send officers to Syria and Lebanon with Rama Duwaji, contradicting Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office on the security detail.
fullText:
The New York Police Department (NYPD) will not provide a security detail to Mayor Zohran Mamdani's wife during her upcoming vacation to two terror hotspots in the Middle East, despite the mayor's office claiming otherwise.

"The NYPD does not send officers to countries with level 4 travel advisories for discretionary reasons such as personal travel," a spokesperson for the law enforcement agency told Fox News.

Mamdani's wife, Rama Duwaji, is planning to travel to Syria and Lebanon to visit family in September, according to the New York Post. Both of those countries are on the State Department's "Do Not Travel" list due to terrorism concerns.

Mamdani's Wife Co-hosts Luxe Muslim Retreat Casting Virgin Mary As 'Palestinian Woman' Under Occupation

The mayor's office had previously confirmed that Duwaji would have an NYPD security detail on the trip.

"Upon the strong recommendation of the NYPD, the first lady's security detail will be joining her when she travels to visit family in Syria and Lebanon," Mamdani's spokeswoman Dora Pekec reportedly said.

But later, as it became clear that the NYPD would not be making the overseas trek, the mayor chalked the confusion up to a staff "miscommunication" when asked about it by news outlet PIX11 on Tuesday.

NYPD Detectives' Endowment Association (DEA) President Scott Munro furiously slammed the implication that NYPD detectives would accompany the city's First Lady to the Middle East.

"Our detectives put themselves in harm's way every day protecting New Yorkers," said Munro. "The DEA would never remain silent if our members were asked to travel to a dangerous, off-limits foreign country for anything other than a legitimate law-enforcement or intelligence operation."

title: Meta CTO told employees AI gains should go into more work
description: Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth told staff that AI productivity gains should go into building more products, not more vacation. He called the question "very dumb."
fullText:
Meta CTO Bosworth told employees AI gains should go into more work, not more time off. Called the Meta Days vacation question “very dumb.” Meta cut 8,000 jobs this year while spending $135B on AI.

Meta’s chief technology officer Andrew Bosworth told employees at a July Q&A that AI productivity gains should be used to build more products, not to take more time off. An employee had asked whether the gains could be channelled into reviving “Meta Days,” a cancelled holiday programme that gave staff a few extra days off. Bosworth’s answer was blunt: “Stop asking about Meta Days. It’s very dumb.”

“I hope that what we do with our extra time is do even more and cooler stuff for the users who use our products every day,” Bosworth said, according to three people on the call. “I get an extra hour. You know what I do with it? I put it into that.” He told the employee to ask their parents what they would think of using every chance to talk to a boss to request more days off. He later said he was sorry for coming down “too hard” and acknowledged the question may have been “tongue-in-cheek.”

The comments land in a specific context. Meta cut 8,000 jobs in May while spending up to $135 billion on AI infrastructure this year. The company replaced its cancelled Meta Days with two “choice days” and provides four weeks off plus public holidays. Bosworth himself stands to earn up to $921 million from a stock option programme tied to Meta reaching a $9 trillion valuation by 2031. The message to employees is that AI makes them more productive, the company keeps the productivity, and the reward is the privilege of building more.

The broader debate is whether AI productivity gains belong to workers or employers. Jeff Bezos has said he expects AI to let households return to a single earner. Morgan Stanley predicted AI would help millions take on second and third jobs. Bosworth’s position is the employer’s version: more output, same hours, no extra days. At a company that cut 10% of its workforce this year, told survivors to train their AI replacements, and installed keystroke-tracking software on employee laptops, the answer to “can we have more time off?” was always going to be no. Bosworth just said it out loud.

fullText:
Newcastle United fans preparing for the 2026/27 Premier League season.

Less than three weeks to go now until Liverpool travel to St James' Park.

An 'interesting' summer so far…

An ideal time to get a snapshot of views from Newcastle United fans on their thoughts.

So we sent out questions to a number of regular/irregular contributors to The Mag, varying to a degree the questions that different fans received to answer.

Next up answering some questions is Matt Busby said to Joe Harvey…:

Three words to describe how you currently feel as a Newcastle United fan?

Three words to describe Newcastle United now?

Do you see it as good news or bad news that Eddie Howe resigned?

Look, the man walks on water for what he has achieved but the conditions that led to what he achieved have changed. And for that reason, he didn't want to be here any longer. So in the circumstances, it's got to be a good thing he's departed, hasn't it?

Hand on heart, what position do you currently believe Newcastle United are most likely to finish in the 2026/27 Premier League season?

Without the distraction of Europe, we have got to be aiming for a European spot surely?

If Eddie Howe had stayed would your 2026/27 prediction have been different (up or down…)?

I think I've been persuaded that he wasn't up for re-inventing the side so I'd probably suggest we wouldn't finish any higher.

If Bruno leaves, who do you think would be best choice of NUFC captain?

I'd consider giving it to Lewis Hall, assuming he's not bound for pastures new as well. The guy seems as smart off the park as he does on it and I reckon there's a proper leader in there.

The opening six league games are Liverpool home, Spurs away, Bournemouth home, Leeds away, Hull home and Coventry away. How many points would Newcastle need to take for you to be happy and what would you predict will be the reality?

Despite two bogey teams visitingSt James' Park early doors , I think we can win all three home games. I'd also fancy us to pick up another four points from the away trips, so that's 13 from 18, and I'd be very content with that.

(So if you have 100% fears and 0% hopes that would be 100/0, if feeling 60% fear and 40% hope then 60/40)

I reckon 35:65 is my ratio. In other words, whilst I think there's a 1 in 3 chance that we'll blow up, I reckon there's a 2 in 3 chance of us kicking on. As above, if we can plunder 13 points from our first 6 games, any fears I have will be consigned to the dustbin.

Anthony Gordon leaving, your thoughts?

I think he lost faith when we were seemingly prepared to offload him when we hit the PSR buffers in June 2024, and it seems to me that he became selfish and as a result, his form more erratic and the consistency we'd previously seen/expected disappeared somewhat.

Hearing him speak in Spanish when signing for Barcelona seemed to reinforce the fact that he was hell bent on leaving us for Iberia.

When the lad was on fire, he was great, and it might be that the £70 million the Catalans have paid is seen as a steal, but he had a tendency to lose his head when the stakes were high and the history books will show he wasn't on the park when we lifted our first trophy in donkey's years (despite his endeavour in both legs of the semi final).

Long winded way of me saying, I'm not too concerned that AG has left Newcastle United.

Hornicek, Hall, Livramento, Botman and Thiaw – basically, the whole of the defence

One of Osula, Woltemade or Wissa – basically anyone who is deployed to put the ball in the onion bag

Toure and New Signing – two of the new guys

NUFC CEO David Hopkinson said the intention is that by 2030 the club will be competing to win all competitions. What do you make of what he said?

I still think of that ham and egg lawyer, Saul Goodman, played so well by Bob Odenkirk in 'Better call Saul', when I see footage of Hopkinson, so cannot take him too seriously.

That said, 2030 is still four years away and the summer clear out, both on the park and in the dugout, together with Ross Wilson seemingly yielding more power is a statement of sorts.

Let's see what 2026/27 brings first though…..

How would you rate your optimism for next season at Newcastle United from 0-100?

65 – more positive than negative, with those first six games being a helpful barometer

How important (or not) is a huge new stadium for Newcastle United?

Not sure what is meant by huge? I'm assuming 80,000 although I think 65,000 to 70,000 would suffice.

I think it is very important, for three reasons….

First, so we can both generate more cash for investment in the squad (I'm thinking rock concerts and other non-football events as much as I am extra gate receipts). Second, so those who are scrambling for tickets through the ballot system all have a better chance of seeing NUFC play at home. And third, to upgrade the pretty shambolic facilities that currently exist within the confines of SJP.

Whatever the capacity, a new stadium needs to be as close to the current site as possible. I think an out of town complex, however fancy, would rip the soul out of the matchday experience.

Did England have a successful 2026 World Cup finals?

I was so bored of the whole spectacle that by the time England exited in such a limp fashion, I wasn't really bothered.

Some say finishing third is England's best outcome at a World Cup since 1966, so relatively speaking, I suppose they did have a successful tournament.

Bruno Guimaraes wanting to leave Newcastle United after four and a half years, has that changed your opinion of him as a person?

Given most footballers have a tendency of saying anything to curry favour, I'll give Bruno a pass when it comes to his previous proclamations expressing his commitment to the cause.

My question is, did he really want to leave?

On the one hand, he might be thinking there's a greater chance of silverware in north London. On the other, it's pretty obvious we've offloaded our top earners as well as generating some much needed revenue to help combat the problem of SCR.

Whatever the reason, he captained the club to its first silverware in decades, so he's still up there for me and despite seeing him in the red of Arsenal will be a real sickener, I'll give the lad a standing ovation on his return to St James.

I wouldn't be surprised to see him and his old man attending Newcastle United away games in the future.

Maybe with Trump's recent intervention in the middle east, they've got more to be concerned about than using Newcastle United as a vehicle to distract folk from their regime.

Who would you have liked to see replace Eddie Howe, Matthias Jaissle or somebody else?

Tommy Tuchel maybe, until his tactical masterclass against the Argentines?

title: Trump again tries to limit US birthright citizenship with new executive orders
description: The executive orders ban birth tourism and expand the existing definition of people whose children are not eligible for US birthright citizenship.
fullText:
Donald Trump is trying again to scale back birthright citizenship in the US, weeks after the Supreme Court shot down his previous attempt to eliminate the right.

The president signed two executive orders on Thursday, including one that expands the existing definitions of non-citizens whose children are not eligible for birthright citizenship.

The second order bans so-called birth tourism, the practice of pregnant mothers coming to the US to give birth so that their babies will be citizens.

"This should have happened years ago, but we're taking care of it now," Trump said from the Oval Office, criticising the Supreme Court's rejection of his previous bid to end the 150-year-old policy.

"My Administration has guarded against the risks posed by malign foreign actors who attempt to swindle American citizens by taking advantage of the generosity of our Nation," the first executive order says.

That order prohibits the automatic citizenship of babies born in the United States to two non-citizen parents where one of the parents is: a member of a foreign terrorist group, a foreign government employee, has attempted to gain citizenship through fraudulent means, or is living in US territories where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute.

Birthright citizenship for people born in US territories such as Puerto Rico is codified by federal statute.

Trump and members of his administration have repeatedly railed against birth tourism, including accusing Russian and Chinese adversaries of taking advantage of birthright citizenship to infiltrate the US.

While announcing the executive orders from the Oval Office on Thursday, Trump said that hundreds of thousands of babies have been born through birth tourism in the US.

The Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan research group, has said that the most expansive census-based estimate accounts for about 22,000 to 26,000 babies born in the US from birth tourism every year. Government data, according to the institute, showed that there were 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024.

"The idea (is) that people come here pretending to be a tourist, pretending to be a visitor," Stephen Miller, homeland security advisor and White House deputy chief of staff for policy, said while standing beside the president on Thursday.

"But the real reason they're here is to have a child, to make that child an automatic citizen, (to) leave our country and then have a US citizen child," he said, adding that thoe children then gain access to welfare benefits, the voting booth, and "all the other rights and privileges that belong solely to Americans".

Miller said the president has the authority to ban birth tourism under a section of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which grants the president the power to set exceptions and limitations on who can enter into the country.

On one of his first back days in office in 2025, Trump signed an executive order that tried to end birthright citizenship as guaranteed in the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution.

A legal battle brought the case to the Supreme Court, which in June ruled that Trump's 2025 policies could not stand and birthright citizenship remained the law.

The decision was a major blow to Trump's ongoing efforts to limit who can live, work, and become citizens in the US.

The high court made "a bad decision, very unfair decision", Trump said from the Oval Office on Thursday while announcing the executive orders. "Our country suffers because of it, and we're ending in a different way."

fullText:
Trump’s FCC is developing a measure to bar US imports of new models of Chinese datacenter devices, sources say

The Trump administration is reportedly drafting a ban on US imports of new models of Chinese datacenter components, in the latest sign US authorities are scrambling to respond to the rapid development of AI technology in China.

Four people familiar with the matter told Reuters that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which oversees the US ⁠telecommunications industry, is developing a measure to bar imports of new ​Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light within datacenters. Officials hope to publish the measure this year, according to Reuters.

The FCC could still modify or shelve the restriction, Reuters reported. But the deliberations are the latest example that the Trump administration is increasingly focused on limiting Chinese technological incursions into cutting-edge US industries.

The US has long been at the forefront of the AI industry, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google driving the development of models, and chipmakers such as Nvidia commanding the chip supply chain.

But advancements in China’s artificial intelligence, chip manufacturing and robotics technologies have rattled markets, caused divisions among US tech moguls and left the Trump administration scrambling to respond.

Chinese companies are some of the biggest manufacturers of components necessary for datacenters, with the country’s optical transceiver industry controlling a majority of the global market for the technology. US tech companies have committed trillions of dollars to build out American AI infrastructure. Plans for that buildout are broadly falling behind schedule, however, while China attempts to catch up with its own massive development of datacenters.

Chinese datacenter components are of concern because they could allow Chinese firms to steal ⁠data, install malware or disrupt service in the US if they are embedded in US infrastructure, experts say.

Last month, the FCC announced a ban on China’s advanced humanoid robots. The Trump administration is also reportedly mulling whether to restrict the use of Chinese open-source AI models.

US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as rationale for those measures. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.

The White House and the FCC did not respond to requests for comment.

The Chinese embassy in Washington told Reuters that Beijing ‌urges the US to “heed the objective and rational voices of the business communities in both countries” and “stop smearing Chinese companies and threatening them with sanctions”.

“China will take all necessary measures in response to any action that causes material harm to its interests,” it added.

Some Trump administration officials have been citing the example of Huawei, a Chinese telecom company, to argue for the new restrictions. Huawei’s equipment was so deeply embedded in US infrastructure that efforts to remove it were difficult.

A US ‌ban on new models of Chinese datacenter devices would probably hit China’s Zhongji Innolight, one of the biggest global sellers of transceivers, which was added to the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies in June.

fullText:
Aug. 1—A scary incident overseas this summer ironically gave Cincinnati Bengals tight end Erick All Jr. the assurance he needed in his comeback from 2024 knee surgery.

Now in his first training camp back, the Fairfield High School graduate is anxious to go full throttle while the Bengals are easing him into the mix, despite being fully cleared.

All was walking along the sidewalk in Greece when a three-wheel truck — which he described as similar to a moped — slammed into him, tossing him to the ground. He bounced up with just some scrapes on his face and a couple bumps and bruises.

What could have been a really bad accident actually helped All regain confidence after a brutal first two years in the NFL. Midway through his rookie season in 2024, he retore the ACL he injured in college and missed the entire 2025 campaign as well.

"I got up and was like, 'I'm (expletive) ready, I'm ready,'" All said. "And it didn't hurt me at all. But it just kind of gave me that confidence, like, 'Oh, I'm back.'"

All said the driver had swerved to avoid colliding with someone else as he was about to cross the street, and the three-wheeler ended up hitting him pretty hard, like he was getting blocked by a defensive tackle.

It felt like a football play, but All is used to being the one tossing opponents to the ground.

"That did a lot of good things for the mental, I'm telling you," All said. "Because that's what I do. I'm here for the physicality, and so, you know, after not playing for a while, and I got smacked by that thing, and I got up, 'I'm like, that's as big of a hit that anybody could give.' That's the first time I ever got pancaked, ever, and so I'm like, 'If I can take that, I'm good.' I'm usually the hammer."

All said his friends were stunned he was OK. Maybe it shouldn't have been so surprising.

Bengals coach Zac Taylor has said the physicality that All brings is what makes him such an asset in the tight end room.

"He loves football, and he loves the physical portion of football," Taylor said earlier this summer. "The word 'physical' in the dictionary is a picture of Erick All trying to put his face through somebody's soul, and that's the best way I can describe him."

fullText:
The tourism industry continues to navigate a turbulent period with soaring jet fuel prices and the knock-on effect on travel costs. But amid all this, how is Europe faring?

Pretty well, or to be precise, “steady”, according to the Travel Insights 2026: Focus on Europe report published by Amadeus Travel Intelligence and UN Tourism.

Latest findings reveal that the continent remains resilient and continues to "hold up well overall", with passenger traffic having grown 2.3% as well as hotel occupancy up 2% from May 2025 to April 2026 compared to the year prior.

Europe remains the world’s largest tourism destination region, welcoming more than 130 million international tourists in the first quarter of 2026.

Reflecting a 4% increase, this builds on the “strong momentum of 2025”, the report said, with some European destinations having “benefitted from the redirection of tourism flow in March”.

Southern Mediterranean Europe and Northern Europe both saw a 4% increase in arrivals in Q1 2026, while Central Eastern Europe (+6%) consolidated its rebound. Arrivals in Western Europe recorded 2% growth in the first quarter of the year.

Forecast air passenger volume and scheduled airline seats from April to September 2026 are expected to peak at just over 160 million, with the US, Spain and Germany being among the largest markets.

Aside from these top three, the report also found the strongest year-on-year growth from Japanese, Danish and Egyptian travellers to Europe at 19%, 11% and 8% respectively.

With regards to origin markets, Japanese travellers are the most likely to “pack their bags and travel to Europe”, the report said. A 62% growth in search from Japan translated into a 19% growth in bookings, surpassing Denmark, the next origin market in terms of bookings growth, by eight percentage points.

Just where is everyone travelling to?

Spain dominates as being both Europe's most searched-for and booked destination. However, Czechia ranked number one as the fastest‑growing booked destination among Europe’s top markets with year-on-year growth at 18%, ahead of Iceland on 11%.

The country also ranks highly among the top searched-for destinations within Central and Eastern Europe as well as hotel occupancy having risen from a 2026 new year slump to more than 60%.

Other destinations, including Iceland and Denmark, are also recording the strongest growth among the continent’s 30 most booked destinations.

According to the report, this signals a strong appetite among travellers for culturally rich city breaks and nature‑led travel in Northern and Central Europe, pointing to a shift away from what it calls “traditional tourism powerhouses”. The booking data also shows travellers are on the hunt for destinations that offer distinct experiences alongside seasonal balance.

Meanwhile, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan emerged as capturing travellers' attention online the most, with searches for both countries climbing 64%. Strong search growth also came from Switzerland (+36%), Sweden (+36%), Denmark (+34%), Ireland (+33%), Belgium (+32%) and Norway (+31%).

Arrivals to Southern and Mediterranean Europe across July and August will reach a peak of almost 70 million in air passenger volume and scheduled airline seats.

Compared to anywhere else on the continent, the South and Mediterranean region is expanding air connectivity the most. Around 1,100 new flight routes have been launched in the past year, with 96 hailing from Germany, 58 from France and 51 from Italy and Spain. Among the emerging links are Slovakia to Spain, Ethiopia to Portugal, as well as China to Greece.

The report also found that travellers are booking their holidays well in advance. More than half of bookings, around 53%, to the South and Mediterranean region are made at least one month before departure, with the 61- to 180-day booking window accounting for around 26%, which is the largest share.

However, the region does still also see last-minute travel demand with around 29% of trips being made between one and 14 days before departure, with another 17% of travellers arriving 15 to 30 days from booking.

“Travellers are actively booking close to departure, creating space for flash promotions, weekend packages and dynamic pricing aimed at flexible last-minute demand," the report said.

Who says wanderlust fades as you get older?

Europe-wide, adults aged 46 to 65 now account for approximately 30% of travel demand across the continent, which is the largest traveller demographic by age. This figure even increases slightly in destinations such as London, Paris and Madrid.

A previous report by Amadeus found that this demographic is especially interested in authentic local experiences, cultural discovery, wellbeing and a deeper connection to destinations.

“This mature, high-spending audience is well aligned with premium experiences and cultural offerings, while younger groups still hold meaningful share to support a multigenerational visitor mix,” the Travel Insights 2026 report said.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Stuart Fails to Save the Universe' You Should Watch Next
description: More high-concept sci-fi shows featuring time travel, multiverses, and more.
fullText:
Not since Happy Days spun off into Mork and Mindy has there been a weirder TV franchise expansion than Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, which takes the relatively straightforward sitcom antics of The Big Bang Theory and expands them into the multiverse. It seems that, at some point after the conclusion of their show, Howard, Sheldon, and Leonard built a quantum something-or-other machine that went haywire and triggered a multiversal apocalypse that only comic book guy Stuart (Kevin Sussman) can stop.

It's early days yet, but the HBO series is pretty fun, making the most of the parent show's geeky bona fides and affection for genre tropes. If you're looking for more entertainment in the same nerdy vein, here are other shows that inject varying degrees of comedy into serious sci-fi scenarios.

Though less overtly comedic, there's an appealing goofiness to this quintessentially '90s bit of sci-fi, a show that anticipates the multiversal mayhem of the modern Marvel era. Jerry O'Connell is Quinn Mallory, who accidentally opens a portal that sends him and a rotating group of companions (including, initially, John Rhys-Davies as Quinn's mentor) through the multiverse. The device that he invents to get them all home is, inconveniently, an unreliable timer that keeps them stuck wherever they land for...well, however much time the story demands. Over the course of their adventures, they visit worlds where the Soviet Union won the Cold War, where antibiotics were never invented, and where Hillary Clinton is president (I swear!). Increasing serialization involving a whole species of mostly evil sliders doesn't really improve things as the show goes on, but it's still a pretty good time. Stream Sliders on Peacock and Tubi.

Josh Hutcherson plays Josh Futturman, a twenty-something janitor who lives with his parents and isn't good at much aside from video games. Though that's enough, as it turns out: He's the only person ever to finish the game Biotic Wars, a success that triggers the arrival of time-traveling soldiers from the future who recruit Josh for their war (yes, that's basically the plot of The Last Starfighter). The show succeeds by wearing its sci-fi influences on its sleeve, taking its world and backstory seriously before populating it with goofy, raunchy, and believably out-of-their-depth characters. Buy Future Man from Prime Video.

The subject here is outer-space sci-fi in the Star Trek mold, but it's still a beautifully irreverent sendup of the genre, with an amiable loser at its center. Craig Charles is Dave Lister, a well-meaning slob who holds the lowest job possible on the enormous mining ship Red Dwarf. When he sneaks a pregnant cat aboard, he's punished by being placed in suspension (without pay) for the rest of the trip. Which is a lot longer than anyone anticipated: When Dave wakes up, three million years have passed, and humanity is entirely extinct. The kittens survived and sired an inbred cat empire that's since risen and all but fallen, while the senile main computer has recreated Dave's hated roommate (Chris Barrie) as a hologram to keep him company. Soon joined by a prissy android, they spend the next 30+ years bumming about in space and stumbling into adventures. Stream Red Dwarf on Britbox.

In a depressingly straight and self-serious superhero-media landscape, Legends of Tomorrow soared past its rocky origins as a dumping ground for supporting characters from other DC shows to become something altogether weirder (and queerer). Initially recruited by a time traveller for a mission specifically because of their insignificance (their absences from the timeline won't affect a thing), the Legends go from screwups to reluctant heroes under the leadership of Sara Lance (Caity Lotz), putting things right in time and space. Blending solid character work with brilliant goofiness, the show saw plotlines involving a giant animatronic bear threatening the Old West, a season-ending fight scene set to "The Thong Song," and a character's nipple getting bitten off by a unicorn. Stream Legends of Tomorrow on Netflix.

I feel like Resident Alien flew a bit under the radar during its run, though it still managed a solid four-season run. Alan Tudyk (Serenity, Rogue One, Superman) stars as Dr. Harry Vanderspeigle, sort of: He's actually an alien with an unpronounceable name who crashed on Earth before killing the real Harry and assuming his identity. He's meant to scout the planet for a planned destruction, but, by assuming human form and integrating with the community in the tiny town of Patience, Colorado, he slowly begins to have second thoughts, even as he continues to be entirely repulsed by human culture. Tudyk is genuinely funny while managing to hit some moving emotional beats along his journey to not-wanting-to-kill-us-all-quite-as-much, and the supporting cast is similarly game. The fictional setting is set near the real Southern Ute Reservation, and offers up some impressive Indigenous representation, including Sara Tomko as Harry's bestie and occasional foil, Asta Twelvetrees. Stream Resident Alien on Peacock and Netflix.

The Librarians began life as a charming, Indiana Jones-light TV movie led by Noah Wylie way back in 2004, which spawned two sequels, the series in question, as well as a sequel show now entering its second season. While largely a standalone take on the mildly comedic premise (a secret annex of the New York Public Library that catalogs magical and occult objects), The Librarians finds Rebecca Romjin, John Larroquette, and Christian Kane leading a group of action-scholars who use their brains to save the world. They're not lovable losers in the Stuart mode, but are, nonetheless, a bunch of true nerds who become reluctant heroes. Stream The Librarians on Prime Video.

Creator Will Forte stars as Phil Miller, a former banker who believes, for about a year, that he’s the only survivor of a plague that wiped out humanity...until he meets Kristen Schaal, a notary from Delaware. The two don’t have much in common, but decide they’re responsible for repopulating the earth. Frequently genuinely funny, the show winds up striving for a larger purpose than parodying end-of-the-world narratives, exploring our obsession with the end times and what it means to live in a world where apocalyptic thinking winds up becoming self-fulfilling. Stream The Last Man on Earth on Hulu.

The tone of this sensational series is wildly different than that of Stuart, and yet it would feel like a disservice to not mention this weird sci-fi apocalypse from Breaking Bad's Vince Gilligan, which displays a very dark, very dry sense of humor. Rhea Seehorn plays Carol Sturka, a fantasy romance author and general grouch who becomes one of only 13 people on the planet immune to the "Joining"—the result of an alien virus that transforms the rest of humanity into a peaceful, perky, and perpetually content hive mind. Carol refuses to surrender her miserableness in the face of a loss of identity, fighting instead to restore humanity to its admittedly cruddy ways. Saving the world means saving the world for snobby misanthropes like herself. Thrilling, heartbreaking, and genuinely funny, the show manages to address some big questions about what it means to be human, and what we'd be willing to give up to change. Stream Pluribus on Apple TV.

Based on the ‘90s-era vehicular combat games that your parents probably hated (involving, as they do, a lot of wild, demolition-derby style action in which you smash and/or blow up your opponents), Twisted Metal stars Anthony Mackie as John Doe, a driver tasked with carrying a package across the entirely lawless Wasteland while dodging challenges that include a murderous clown in an ice cream truck. Alternately brutal and goofy, the show mostly does what it says on the tin, providing plenty of frenetic car-on-car action (and car-on-semi, car-on-hearse, -ice cream truck, etc.). If the over-the-top comedic violence of Stuart is your bag, you'll get plenty of that here. Stream Twisted Metal on Peacock.

New Queer Cinema pioneer Greg Araki followed up his neon-tinged cinematic apocalypse in Kaboom with Now Apocalypse, a successor in spirit. Avan Jogia plays Ulysses Zane, living in sun-soaked California with his best friend Carly (Kelli Berglund), a struggling actress and sex worker. He keeps having bizarre dreams about an alien invasion that feel increasingly like they might be premonitions, or possibly just anxiety delusions brought on by too much weed. The show only lasted one season and never quite made it to its own prophesied apocalypse, but it was definitely fun while it lasted, and definitely offers something a bit to the left of the typical dreary end-of-the-world. It's a comedy dystopia, just sweatier and hornier than usual. Stream Now Apocalypse on Tubi.

title: Search intensifies for North Carolina physical therapist who vanished during Caribbean getaway
description: Authorities are searching for missing North Carolina physical therapist Elizabeth Waddell after she vanished during a vacation in Grenada near Grand Anse Beach.
fullText:
A North Carolina woman has vanished while on a trip to the Caribbean island of Grenada, sparking an urgent search as her family, friends and loved ones plead for her safe return.

Elizabeth "Liz" Waddell, 44, was last seen Wednesday at Grand Anse Beach in St. George's, near where she was staying in the Grand Anse area, according to the Royal Grenada Police Force.

Waddell, a physical therapist, wife and mother from the Raleigh area, is described as 5 feet 5 inches tall with short blonde hair. Authorities also released a photo showing Waddell with pink hair as they asked the public for help locating her.

According to her professional website, Waddell is the founder of Art of Movement Physical Therapy and earned a doctorate in physical therapy from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

Search Underway For Australian Woman Who Vanished After Sending Message About Going For A Hike Near Las Vegas

According to a friend who said she has known Waddell and her husband for more than 20 years, Waddell traveled to Grenada for a vacation with another friend, WRAL News reported.

Waddell's friend reportedly lost sight of her after remaining at their Airbnb to take an online course while Waddell went outside, apparently for a swim.

"She had her swimsuit on, and she went outside their Airbnb," Amanda Romano-Harmon said, according to the local outlet. "They had a pool that overlooked the bay. Liz was set up out there just sightseeing from the pool, and her friend was taking her online course. When she got through with her course, she looked up and she didn't see Liz outside, so she went outside to walk around and see where she went, and she saw her towel down on the pier. So the only thing we can think is maybe she went for a swim."

The friend reportedly became increasingly concerned over the next several hours, knowing Waddell did not have her phone with her, and eventually filed a missing-persons report.

Three Sisters Found Dead In Ocean At Popular Tourist Beach As Police Probe Mysterious Tragedy

Waddell's husband, Cailen, was at work when he received the call about his wife's disappearance, according to the report.

He said on social media Friday that he was heading to the area to assist in the search and urged anyone with connections to the island to share information that could help locate her.

He also described Waddell as a kind-hearted person while speaking with local Grenada media outlets.

"My wife is a loving, free-spirited person. She could make friends with anyone. She often did," he told Grenada Broadcasting Network (GBN).

Police are urging anyone with information about Waddell's whereabouts to come forward, specifically asking fishermen, boat operators and residents along Grenada's southern coastline to report any sightings that could assist in the search.

Kentucky Man Charged With Boating Under The Influence After Female Passenger, 19, Goes Missing

According to GBN, an extensive search effort is underway with the assistance of police officers, divers and students from St. George's University.

The U.S. State Department told Fox News Digital on Sunday that officials are aware of reports of a missing American citizen in Grenada and emphasized that the Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of U.S. citizens abroad.

The State Department declined to provide additional details due to privacy considerations but said it can assist families and friends with filing missing persons reports and help them understand local procedures.

Aradia Fitness, where Waddell also works as a fitness instructor,  called the news of her disappearance "disheartening" in a social media post and said the community is praying for her safe return.

Anyone with information is urged to contact the South Saint George Police Station at 444-4454, the Criminal Investigation Department at 440-3921, the police emergency line at 911, or the nearest police station, the Royal Grenada Police Force said.

fullText:
BEIJING (AP) — China said on Saturday it had imposed penalties of nearly 5.2 billion yuan ($765 million) on Trip.com Group, which operates the country's largest online travel platform, over claims of monopolistic conduct.

Trip.com, which runs Ctrip and Skyscanner among other brands, was said to be restricting market competition through means such as entering into exclusive partnerships with some hotels and offering prioritized traffic allocation to them, China's State Administration for Market Regulation said in a statement.

It prohibited some hotels from collaborating with competing platforms, the regulator added, and had also demanded some hotel operators who were operating on multiple platforms to ensure the rates for their platform were the lowest available online.

The regulator said Trip.com had been abusing its dominant market position in the sector since as early as 2020.

The regulator, which started its investigation against Trip.com in January, said it had confiscated "illegal gains" of more than 1.6 billion yuan ($245 million) from the group and had imposed a fine of over 3.5 billion yuan ($520 million).

The company was also asked to refund about 122 million yuan ($18 million) which it was withholding from hotel operators.

Trip.com's behavior had "eliminated and restricted market competition, constrained hotel operators from conducting cross-platform business, infringed upon hotel operators' right to set their own prices and harmed consumer interests," the regulator's statement said.

title: Mexican man killed after ICE encounter in Florida was on vacation, officials say
description: — A Mexican man who was struck and killed by a tractor trailer in Florida after running from federal immigration officers was vacationing in the U.S. and had a tourist visa, according to a ...
fullText:
A Mexican man who was struck and killed by a tractor trailer in Florida after running from federal immigration officers was vacationing in the United States and had a tourist visa, according to a Mexico official and a group assisting his wife.

Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, 28, died July 14 after authorities said he darted across a busy road in St. Augustine and into the path of a truck. His death was the third in roughly a week involving encounters with Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, following fatal shootings in Texas and Maine.

Coronilla Durán traveled from his hometown of San Luis de la Paz, in the central Mexican state of Guanajuato, to Atlanta to visit family and friends, according to Isaret Jeffers, founder of Colectivo Arbol, a farmworkers advocacy group. He had stayed in Georgia for three weeks before traveling to Florida's east coast to enjoy the beaches, Jeffers said Tuesday.

US authorities have not publicly identified the man, but a Mexico official confirmed his name. Jeffers said Yezzika Alamilla, the man's wife, told them he had been visiting the US on a tourist visa.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday about whether Coronilla Durán had a valid visa.

Coronilla Durán was one of four people in a vehicle that stopped in a gas station parking lot before 7 a.m. on the day he died. The four fled on foot during an encounter with agents from ICE and Homeland Security Investigations, with one darting across a busy road into the path of the semi, the Florida Highway Patrol said.

It is unclear what prompted the encounter and what happened to the vehicle's other three occupants.

The Highway Patrol and DHS have not provided additional details, citing the ongoing investigation.

Alamilla called Colectivo Arbol, which provides legal advice and assistance to farmworkers in Central Florida, the day after her husband died, Jeffers said. She was seeking help to travel from Mexico and repatriate her husband's remains. The organization bought her a plane ticket and put her up for three days, until Monday, she said. The Mexican consulate has been helping her since.

"His wife said he was there on a tourist visa. She didn't understand what was happening," Jeffers said. "He didn't come to work; he wasn't working. He was here as a tourist."

Alamilla "thinks he was very afraid, and that's why he ran away," Jeffers said.

According to information provided by the widow, Coronilla Durán "had been in the United States for only a very short time (and) had a tourist visa," said Susana Guerra Vallejo, the undersecretary for assistance to migrants and mobility issues for the Mexican state of Guanajuato.

She said that Alamilla would be able to see the body of her husband at the Florida funeral home.

Coronilla Durán's body will be transported to Mexico on a commercial flight from Orlando, Guerra Vallejo told The Associated Press. He will be buried in his hometown of San Luis de la Paz, a farming community in Guanajuato that is about 160 miles northwest of Mexico City, she said.

Coronilla Durán and Alamilla had two children, a 7-month-old girl and a 7-year-old boy, Jeffers said.

Coronilla Durán's death was at least the 10th involving encounters with immigration agents since President Donald Trump launched his mass deportation campaign last year.

The Mexican government said it had asked state attorneys general in the US to review the deaths of migrants in ICE custody or during raids for possible criminal prosecution.

title: Christian lawmaker says UK barred her from entering country after Finland 'hate speech' conviction
description: Finnish lawmaker Päivi Räsänen says her U.K. travel authorization was canceled after disclosing her hate speech conviction over biblical views.
fullText:
A Finnish Christian lawmaker says British authorities revoked her permission to travel to the United Kingdom following her recent "hate speech" conviction over statements expressing biblical views on marriage and sexuality, raising fresh concerns among religious freedom advocates about the consequences of the ruling.

Päivi Räsänen, a member of Finland's Parliament and the country's former interior minister, said her previously approved U.K. Electronic Travel Authorization was canceled without explanation, jeopardizing plans to speak at events in Northern Ireland next month. Räsänen is appealing her conviction to the European Court of Human Rights.

A screenshot of the cancellation message shared with Fox News Digital read, "Dear ETA Customer, The information you provided in your ETA application suggests that you are not eligible for an ETA and it has been cancelled. If you still want to travel to the UK, you will need to apply or reapply for one of the following: Electronic Travel Authorisation Standard visitor visa Transit visa Temporary work – creative worker visa."

Hasan Piker Says Uk Has Barred Him, Trashes 'Unbelievable...power' Of Pro-israel Groups

"I tried to apply for an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) from the United Kingdom authorities because of my future travels to UK," Räsänen told Fox News Digital in a statement.

"As part of the application process, I was asked to disclose any criminal convictions within the past 12 months. At first, I got a positive answer on 17th June, but on 3rd July I got a shocking message from GOV.UK that my application was cancelled, 'The information you provided in your ETA application suggests that you are not eligible for an ETA and it has been cancelled.'"

According to Alliance Defending Freedom, who has been representing Räsänen in litigation, in 2019 she criticized her church's sponsorship of an LGBT event in a post on X that included a passage from Romans 1. Finnish prosecutors later charged her with "agitation against a minority group" under the country's criminal code, citing the social media post, a 2004 church pamphlet she wrote about marriage and sexuality, and remarks she made during a 2019 radio discussion.

Bible Verse Leads To Trial In Europe. Growing Crackdown Threatens Our Us-uk Values

Räsänen told Fox News Digital Monday that she had planned to travel to Northern Ireland in August to speak at the Bangor Worldwide Missionary Convention about free speech and faith. She also said the cancellation has already affected her travel plans, forcing her to reroute a recent return trip from California through Dallas rather than connecting through London's Heathrow Airport.

"On 26 March 2026, I was convicted by a narrow 3–2 majority decision of the Supreme Court over statements expressing biblical views on marriage and sexuality in a booklet I wrote in 2004," Räsänen said.

Her booklet is called, "Male and Female He Created Them," and Räsänen said she was sentenced to a total of 20 days' wages worth of fines.

Räsänen said she plans to challenge the decision before the European Court of Human Rights, arguing authorities failed to properly consider her rights to free speech and religious freedom under the European Convention on Human Rights. She said the cancellation has had broader consequences than she anticipated, affecting not only her ability to express her views but also complicating international travel and participation in conferences.

"My greatest concern is that this decision has left many people with uncertainty, confusion, and fear about the consequences of exercising their freedom of speech and faith in a peaceful manner, and about where the line lies between lawful and prohibited speech," Räsänen said.

"Also Lutheran Bishop Juhana Pohjola, who was convicted alongside me because of publishing my booklet, has been denied the travel authorization ETA," she added. "However, I trust that all of this is in God's hands, and I pray that He leads and guides in the way He wills. During these seven years, I have witnessed how the Lord miraculously turns evil things into good."

Räsänen said she has longstanding ties to the United Kingdom through her parliamentary work, including membership in the Finland–United Kingdom friendship group and previous visits as both a member of Parliament and Finland's interior minister.

She said she plans to travel to the U.K. again for official duties and currently serves on Finland's Foreign Affairs Committee, the country's delegation to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly and the board of its Inter-Parliamentary Union group.

Gop Lawmakers Urge Supreme Court To Strengthen First Amendment Protections For Street Preachers

Räsänen added that she has contacted the U.K. Home Office and written to Shabana Mahmood, secretary of state for the Home Department, seeking a response, but has not yet received one.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Lorcan Price, senior legal counsel at Alliance Defending Freedom said, "The refusal of a travel authorization for Päivi Räsänen is the latest example of the United Kingdom government's authoritarian attempt to suppress any speech or speaker they disagree with."

Price added, "The fact that Päivi was due to address a conference on the theme of religious freedom makes this all the more ironic and outrageous. The UK government has shown contempt for freedom of expression, and this is just the latest example."

Fox News Digital reached out to the U.K. Home Office and Mahmood for comment.

title: Rebecca Lowe details how helicopter ride nearly derailed entire Fox World Cup broadcast
description: Those who tuned in for Fox’s four-hour World Cup final pregame show on Sunday witnessed Rebecca Lowe and the rest of the network’s studio crew travel by land, air, and sea to make it from Brooklyn Bridge Park to MetLife Stadium in time for kickoff. What viewers might not have realized is how the intricate…
fullText:
Those who tuned in for Fox’s four-hour World Cup final pregame show on Sunday witnessed Rebecca Lowe and the rest of the network’s studio crew travel by land, air, and sea to make it from Brooklyn Bridge Park to MetLife Stadium in time for kickoff. What viewers might not have realized is how the intricate plan to transport the crew almost went entirely wrong.

Fox began coverage of the World Cup final with Lowe, Thierry Henry, Zlatan Ibrahimović, and Alexi Lalas live from a set located in Brooklyn Bridge Park, providing a stunning backdrop for the network’s 2026 World Cup swan song. Midway through the show, the crew would leave the set, take a ferry across the East River, drive to a helipad, and chopper to another helipad located near MetLife Stadium, where Spain and Argentina would kick off at 3 p.m. ET.

That itinerary did not go as planned.

Lowe, appearing on the After The Whistle podcast, explained how she and her colleagues got massively delayed, causing them to wonder if they’d even make it to the final at all.

“We had to get from Brooklyn Bridge Park all the way to MetLife while we were on air. So we started with a boat from the ferry stop over the East River to another pier, into a car to take us a couple of piers down to the heliport,” Lowe explained. “Now, I’ve been on a helicopter once, and I swore I’d never go on one again, but then Fox Sports employed me for the World Cup, and I said, ‘Sure, that sounds great.’

“So, we get in the helicopter. It’s supposed to be seven minutes. Wasn’t seven minutes, it was 30 minutes. And let’s just say, Zlatan, God bless him, didn’t say a single word. I was pretty close to that as well, pretty scared, not going to lie. We were circling. I kept seeing the Yankee Stadium again and again and again. …Terrifying, and it’s very bumpy up there, and it was horrible. Alexi Lalas, I’ve never seen him happier. Out the window, pointing out all the amazing sights and sounds, I was like, ‘This guy.’

“We eventually land at the wrong helipad. So now we’re at a random- by the way, we had to be back on air at 1:15. We eventually get out, we film our little link, and eventually realize we’re not at Teterboro, I think is it called? We’re in Kearny, New Jersey. We didn’t know where we were. We were supposed to meet a police escort, a couple of cars, to take us then to MetLife. Well, they were at Teterboro. So now we’re calling them, they come to get us, that’s 15 minutes. We’re filming another piece just saying, ‘We don’t know where we are.’

“And at this point, I’m thinking, ‘Are we going to make it?’ And at this point, we’re about an hour and a half before kickoff of a World Cup final, and I’m thinking, ‘I’ve done this World Cup for 39 days, and I’m not going to get to do the final because I’m going to be in a car on the New Jersey Turnpike.’

“So at this point … we have to be on air for 1:54. So we get into the police escort, we were going 105 miles an hour. 105. And it was very scary. So that was the helicopter — scary. Then we had the police escort — scary. Then we finally get there, we circle the stadium a couple times because no one knows how to get into this place. Pull up, we go under, we get on the elevator, it’s now 1:51. I go on the set at 1:52. We go on air at 1:54.”

It seems like Murphy’s Law hit the Fox Sports World Cup studio at the worst possible time. Luckily, the team was able to make it to the stadium about an hour before the match started, and the only collateral damage from the entire affair was missing an interview with Timothée Chalamet. Oh, well. That’ll just have to wait until 2030.
